analysis.one_liner: Restores the ban on exporting American crude oil and natural gas.
analysis.headline: The bill to reinstate the crude oil and natural gas export ban never received a committee hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would reverse the 2015 decision that lifted the ban on shipping American crude oil and natural gas to foreign buyers. It directs the President to write a rule prohibiting those exports, with limited exemptions for cases the President finds to be in the national interest, and gives the President optional authority to restrict exports of coal and petroleum products as well. The bill never moved past its initial referral to the Senate Banking Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, American households and businesses would be first in line for domestically produced crude oil and natural gas, which supporters argue would keep more supply at home rather than shipping it overseas. Domestic manufacturers and utilities that burn gas could benefit from larger domestic supply. The bill also preserves the President's flexibility to exempt exports that serve the national interest, such as shipments to close allies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US consumers of oil and gas

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President to issue a rule prohibiting the export of crude oil and natural gas produced in the United States, reversing the 2015 law that lifted the ban.
Allows the President to exempt specific exports if they are found consistent with the national interest and the purposes of the act, including by destination country or class of buyer.
Gives the President optional authority to restrict exports of coal, petroleum products, natural gas, and petrochemical feedstocks, and of equipment needed for domestic energy production and refining.
Preserves historical trading arrangements with Canada and Mexico so cross-border energy exchanges are not interrupted.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers would lose access to foreign markets for crude oil and exports of liquefied natural gas, reducing their revenue. Oil-producing regions could see reduced drilling activity and related jobs, and exporting countries trading partners could face supply disruptions, which is why exemptions exist.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and exporters

drawbacks.text: Economists generally found that the pre-2015 export ban did not lower US consumer prices, because domestic prices are set by domestic supply and demand while world prices are set globally; a ban can cut producer revenues and drilling employment without delivering cheaper gasoline at home.
The bill concentrates sweeping export-control discretion in the President, including the power to waive normal public notice-and-comment procedures when the President deems it necessary.
Restricting natural gas exports could strain allies who rely on US supplies and invite trade disputes, which is partly why the bill includes exemption authority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's premise, that keeping oil and gas at home protects consumers, is contested: since US gasoline prices track domestic conditions, an export ban may deliver less consumer relief than supporters promise while imposing real costs on producers and energy-producing regions. The exemption authority and Canada/Mexico carve-outs temper the blunt edges, but the core tradeoff is real and the bill does not resolve it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in April 2021, and the committee took no further action on it before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the BAN Oil Exports Act on April 28, 2021, joined by Senators Wyden, Merkley, Sanders, and Warren.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action, hearing, markup, or vote, was ever recorded on the bill through the end of the 117th Congress.
The bill would amend the Energy Policy and Conservation Act to require the President to ban crude oil and natural gas exports, with exemptions available in specified circumstances.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and exporters are better off: the export ban never advanced, so foreign-market sales of US crude and liquefied natural gas continue under current law. Consumers gained nothing, since the bill never received a vote.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the ban on crude oil and natural gas exports.

for.name: Sens. Ron Wyden, Jeff Merkley, Bernie Sanders, and Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no additional senators signed on afterward.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed reinstating export restrictions, having lobbied for years to open crude and LNG export markets after the 2015 repeal of the ban.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were progressive Democrats (three of 48 Senate Democrats plus the chamber's other independent); no Republican and no moderate Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-led Banking Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from selling US crude abroad, cutting into export revenue. Because US fuel prices are set largely at home, the industry would bear the cost while consumers would see limited direct relief.

Exports of US-produced natural gas, including LNG shipments to Europe and Asia, would be prohibited absent a presidential exemption. Allies relying on US gas could be affected, which is why the bill includes exemption authority.
The President could restrict coal and petrochemical feedstock exports but is not required to, so the direct effect depends entirely on presidential action.
Keeping crude and gas at home could enlarge domestic supply available to US refiners, utilities, and industrial users.
